Fig 1: Human Speech Production and Perception
•The fundamental purpose of speech is communication.
•It is produced by the vibration of the air through the vocal folds.
•It is a continuously varying acoustic signal.
•Microphone converts this acoustic signal to electrical and the
loudspeaker converts it back to the acoustic form.
•This form of speech processing is the basis for from Bell’s telephone
as well as today’s devices for recording/transmission/manipulation.
•Every speaker has unique speech production characteristics.
•Every speech has a sequence of sounds called phonemes.
Fig 3: Example of a speech waveform with phonetic labels
•Speech chain is the process of producing and perceiving speech.
a. Formulation of the message in the brain of a talker.
b. Creation of the speech signal.
c. Understanding the speech by a listener.
•Speech signal is a sequence of sounds.
•Each sound is referred as phoneme. (Phonemes are not alphabets.)
•Phonemes are arranged in a specific language rule.
•In most languages, the #phonemes ranges b/w 32 to 64.

noisy airflow source to the vocal tract
•Vocal tract – modulates the airflow from the larynx by shaping the

Vocal Tract: Mechanical body (produce vibration and creates sound)It is a tube of non-uniform cross-sectional area bounded by vocal folds and oral cavity at two ends.a.Vocal Folds/Cords: A pair of muscle in the voice box (larynx). Air from the lungs are vibrated in thevocal folds.Open – no vibration (no sound), Close – vibration of air.b.Articulators: hard palate, tongue, teeth, lips, etc. The shape of the vocal tract changes based on themotion of the articulators. (Vibration + Vocal tract shape →sound/phoneme)
I.Based on the Vocal Fold Vibration:
i.Voiced: Vocal folds →open and close (vibration). The vocal tract tube
is excited by the pulses of air pressure resulting from quasi-periodic
opening and closing of vocal folds. Ex: Vowels /UH/ /IY/ , liquids /W/
ii.Unvoiced: Vocal folds are slightly opened (no vibration). Creates
constriction somewhere in the vocal tract tube and forces the air pass
through that constriction, causing turbulent air airflow. (random noise).
iii. Silence: Vocal folds are fully opened (no vibration)
II. Based on the Constriction of the Vocal Tract Tube:
i.Stops: Tube is fully closed, air burst through the oral cavity.
ii.Fricatives: Tube is partially closed (narrow constriction).
iii. Affricates: Tube is fully closed for sometime, and partially opened
Note: Fricatives, Affricates, and Stops can be Voiced or Unvoiced based
on the vibration of the vocal folds.

Vowels• Largest phoneme• No constriction of airflow• Source – quasi-periodic air puffs• Position of tongue + Roundness of lips = voweli.Position of the tongue →high/low and front/backii.Roundness of lips →rounded/unrounded• Example:i./oo/ in food – high, back, roundedii./I/ in thing – low, front, unrounded
2. Diphthongs• Gliding monosyllabic sound • Start at one articulatory position and moves to another position• Source – quasi-periodic air puffs• Example: day, my, boy, house, air, pure
3. Semivowels• Vowel like nature but function-like consonant• Gliding transition between adjacent phonemes• Source – quasi-periodic air puffs • Example: yes, we, water
Note: Strengths of diphthongs, semivowels, and nasals are less than that of a vowel.
